column2: In whom is all, from whom is all, who is all and on every side, and who is ever all-pervading—homage to him, the Self of all.
Homage to you, Vishvakarman, soul of the universe, source of the universe; you are the release of beings, standing beyond the five.
Homage to you in the three worlds, homage to you beyond the three; homage to you in all directions, for you are the final refuge of all.
Homage to you, revered Vishnu, origin and dissolution of the worlds; you are the doer, Hrishikesha, and the destroyer, unconquered.
Therefore I see your divine states in the three paths, and I see in truth that form of yours which is eternal.
Your head pervades the sky, the goddess Earth is your feet, the three worlds your stride; you are the eternal Purusha.
Those who bow to Achyuta, Govinda, flax-flower-hued and clad in yellow, have no fear.
As truth is made of Vishnu, as the oblation is made of Vishnu, as all is made of Vishnu, so may my sin be destroyed.
To me who have taken refuge in you, a devotee, wishing the desired goal, whatever is best, lotus-eyed one, meditate on that, best of gods.
Thus the womb of knowledge and austerity, the unborn Vishnu, has been praised; may the god worshipped by the sacrifice of speech be pleased, Janardana.
Having said this much, Bhishma, his mind absorbed in him, then made obeisance to Krishna with only "Homage."
Understanding by yoga Bhishma's devotion, Madhava, Hari, went to give him divine knowledge of the three times.
When that sound had ceased, those expounders of Brahma, their throats choked with tears, honoured the greatly wise Bhishma with words.
Praising Keshava, the best of men, those best of Brahmanas also praised Bhishma softly again and again.
Knowing Bhishma's devotion, the best of men suddenly rose, glad, and took to his vehicle.
Keshava and Satyaki went in one chariot, and in another the great souls Yudhishthira and Dhananjaya.
Bhimasena and the twins mounted one chariot, and Kripa, Yuyutsu and the charioteer Sanjaya another chariot.
Those bulls among men set out in chariots like cities, making the earth tremble with the great rumble of the wheels.
Then the best of men, glad, heard the words spoken by the twice-born on the road; with joined palms to the bowing and to others, the slayer of Keshi, delighted, welcomed them.
They went swiftly to Kurukshetra in chariots like cities, adorned with banners and flags, with swift horses.
They descended at Kurukshetra, thick with hair, marrow and bones, where those great-souled kshatriyas had laid down their bodies.
It was heaped like mountains with the bones of elephants, horses and men, strewn with human skulls like conches.
Covered with thousands of pyres, full of armour and weapons, it was like Time's drinking-ground, eaten and cast aside.
Frequented by hosts of spirits and thronged by bands of Rakshasas, seeing Kurukshetra the great chariot-warriors swiftly passed on.
Even as he went, the mighty-armed delight of all the Yadavas told Yudhishthira of the prowess of Jamadagni's son.

These five Rama-lakes are seen from afar, Partha, in which he satisfied his ancestors with kshatriya blood.
mahabharata:12:48.9	Having made the earth free of kshatriyas thrice seven times, the lord Rama then ceased from his work here.

When the seed of the kshatriyas was burned by Rama, bull of the Yadus, how did the kshatriya order arise again, of immeasurable valour?
mahabharata:12:48.12	By the great-souled revered Rama, bull of the Yadus, how was the kshatriya order destroyed and how did it regain its livelihood?
mahabharata:12:48.13	In the Mahabharata war crores of kshatriyas were slain, and yet the earth was again strewn with kshatriyas, best of speakers.
mahabharata:12:48.14	Cut this doubt of mine, Vrishni, whose banner is Tarkshya, for from you comes the supreme tradition, younger brother of Vasava.
[Vaishampayana said:] Then, as he went, the lord, elder brother of Gada, told Yudhishthira of incomparable splendour everything truly, how the earth became filled with kshatriyas.
How crores of kshatriyas were slain by Jamadagni's son, and how those slain in the Bharata war rose again in royal lines.
Jahnu's son was Ajahnu, his son Ballava, and the king Kushika, knower of dharma, was his son.
He practised fierce austerity, equal to the thousand-eyed on earth, thinking, "May I gain an unconquered son, lord of the three worlds."
Seeing him of fierce austerity, the thousand-eyed Purandara himself, being able, came to be his son, Bharata.
The lord of the lords of the world became his son, O king; Gadhi was his name, Kaushika, Pakashasana.
He had a daughter, O king, named Satyavati, whom Gadhi gave to Richika, son of the poet (Ushanas).
Then, pleased, Bhargava (Richika), delight of the Kurus, had a sacrificial porridge cooked for a son, for her and also for Gadhi.
Calling his wife, Richika the Bhargava then said: "This porridge is to be eaten by you, and this one by your mother.
And for you too, auspicious one, this porridge will bring forth a steadfast son endowed with austerity, tranquil, best of the twice-born."
Having said this to his wife, Richika, delight of the Bhrigus, wise, devoted to austerity, went to the forest.
At this very time King Gadhi, intent on pilgrimage, came with his wife to Richika's hermitage.
Taking the two porridges, O king, Satyavati, on her husband's word, calmly and gladly gave one to her mother.
The mother, son of Kunti, gave her own porridge to her daughter, and unknowingly took her daughter's herself.
Then Satyavati bore an embryo that would end the kshatriyas, of blazing body and dreadful aspect.
Seeing her, Richika then by meditation said to his lovely wife, tiger among kings:

You were deceived, auspicious one, by the exchange of the porridge: your mother's son will be a cruel-deeded, mighty one.
mahabharata:12:49.19	And your brother will be born, a Brahmin-like ascetic, for I put all Brahma there by austerity.
So told by her husband, the greatly fortunate Satyavati fell with her head before him, trembling, and said this:
You do not deserve, revered one, to say such a word today; you will get a son unworthy of a Brahmana, great sage.
[Richika said:] "This was not the wish I intended for you, auspicious one; the son will be of fierce deeds; the porridge and the mother are the cause."
[Satyavati said:] "If you wish, sage, you could create worlds, how much more for me; may I get a tranquil, upright son, best of those who recite prayers."
[Richika said:] "I have never before spoken untruth, auspicious one, even in jest; how much less when preparing porridge by placing the fire with mantras."
[Satyavati said:] "Then let it be so; let me have a grandson here, and let me get a tranquil, upright son, best of those who recite prayers."
[Richika said:] "There is no difference to me between son and grandson, lovely one; as you have said, so it shall be, auspicious one."
[Vasudeva said:] Then Satyavati bore the Bhargava son Jamadagni, devoted to austerity, tranquil and calm.
And Gadhi, delight of Kushika, obtained a son Vishvamitra, joined to the company of Brahmin-sages and endowed with Brahma through the universe.
The son of Richika begot Jamadagni, most dreadful, best of those who know all science and master of archery, and Rama, slayer of kshatriyas, blazing like fire.
At this very time the mighty son of Kritavirya, a radiant kshatriya of Haihaya lineage, named Arjuna,
burned the whole earth with her seven islands and cities in battle by the strength of his arms and weapons, and with supreme dharma.
Begged by the thirsty Chitrabhanu (Fire), O Kaurava, the valiant thousand-armed one gave him alms.
Villages, cities, cattle-camps and towns the valiant one burned; Chitrabhanu blazed by his arrows, wishing to burn.
By the power of that lord of men, that great ascetic's fire burned the mountains and forests of Kartavirya.
That Haihaya, kindled by the wind, Chitrabhanu, burned that empty hermitage forest of Varuna's son (Apava).
Then Apava in anger cursed Arjuna, Achyuta, when his hermitage was burned by Kartavirya, valiant one:
Because you did not spare this forest of mine out of delusion, it was burned; therefore Rama will cut off your arms in battle, Arjuna.
Arjuna, great king, was strong, ever tranquil, devoted to Brahmanas, a protector, a giver and a hero, Bharata.
His very strong sons, through the curse, were conceited and cruel always, the cause in the slaying of their father.
They brought the calf of Jamadagni's cow, bull of the Bharatas, without the knowledge of the wise Kartavirya, lord of the Haihayas.
Then Jamadagni's son, endowed with manliness, having cut off Arjuna's arms, brought back the weeping calf to his hermitage from their inner quarters, lord.
Then the sons of Arjuna, assembling, foolish, went to the hermitage of the great-souled Jamadagni, who was not on guard.
They struck his head from his body with arrow-heads, O king, when the great-souled Rama had gone out for firewood and kusha grass.
Then Rama, full of supreme anger at his father's slaying, vowing to make the earth free of kshatriyas, took up his weapon.
Then that tiger of the Bhrigus, valiant, quickly slew in battle Kartavirya's sons and grandsons entirely.
Having slain thousands of Haihayas, full of great anger, the Bhargava made the earth a mire of blood, O king.
Having thus made the earth free of kshatriyas, greatly radiant, filled with compassion, he went to the forest.
Then after some thousands of years had passed, the lord, angry by nature, fell into keen agitation.
Paravasu, Vishvamitra's grandson, son of Raibhya, great ascetic, great king, taunted him in a public assembly:

Rama, the good who assembled at Yayati's fall at the sacrifice—Pratardana and others—were they not kshatriyas?
mahabharata:12:49.51	You are a false-vowed boaster in public assemblies, Rama, who for fear of kshatriya heroes took refuge in a mountain.
Hearing Paravasu, the Bhargava again took up weapons against the earth, spread with hundreds of kshatriyas.
Then those kshatriyas, hundreds of whom had been spared by him, grew, of great valour, and became lords of the earth.
He again quickly slew them, even the children, lord of men; but the earth was again filled with those in the womb.
Each embryo as it was born he slew again; but some kshatriya women then protected some sons.
Having made the earth free of kshatriyas thrice seven times, the lord then gave it to Kashyapa at the end of a horse sacrifice as fee.
Then Kashyapa, wishing to preserve the remainder of the kshatriyas, pointing with his hand and holding the ladle, the glorious one, said:
Go beyond the southern sea, great sage; you must never dwell in my domain, Rama.
Then the ocean made for him the Shurparaka country, and Aparanta, the land beyond, in fear of Jamadagni's son.
Kashyapa, great king, accepting this earth and establishing the Brahmana order, entered the great forest.
Then Shudras and Vaishyas, with none to restrain them in their own duties, took to the wives of the best of the twice-born, bull of the Bharatas.
In a world without a king the weak are oppressed by the stronger, and no one has lordship over his property.
Then in time the earth, not duly protected by dharma-guarding kshatriyas, went down to the nether world.
Then Kashyapa held up the earth with his thigh; as she was sinking, O king, the earth is remembered as Urvi (thigh-born) by that.
Then the goddess Earth, pleading with Kashyapa, begged him, pointing to protectors, for the arm-strong kshatriyas:

Brahmana, there are among men bulls of the kshatriyas protected by me, born in the Haihaya line; let them protect me, sage.
mahabharata:12:49.67	There is a Paurava heir, lord, son of Viduratha, raised by bears on the Riksha mountain, Brahmana.
mahabharata:12:49.68	So, compassionate, the sacrificer Parashara of immeasurable splendour protected Saudasa's heir.
mahabharata:12:49.69	He does all works of that sage like a Shudra; known as Sarvakarma, let him protect me, king.
mahabharata:12:49.70	Shibi's son, greatly radiant, named Gopati, protected in the forest by cows, let him protect me, sage.
mahabharata:12:49.71	Pratardana's son, the greatly renowned Vatsa, raised by calves in the cow-pen, let that king protect me.
mahabharata:12:49.72	The grandson of Dadhivahana, son of Divi-ratha, Anga, protected by Gautama too on the Ganga's bank.
mahabharata:12:49.73	The mighty-armed Brihadratha, honoured on earth for his prosperity, the greatly fortunate one protected on Gridhrakuta by langurs.
mahabharata:12:49.74	In Marutta's line there are three Turvasu kshatriyas, equal in valour to the lord of the Maruts, protected by the ocean.
mahabharata:12:49.75	These kshatriya heirs, famed here and there, let them rightly protect me; then I shall stand unmoving.
mahabharata:12:49.76	Their fathers and grandfathers were slain in battle for my sake by Rama of untroubled deeds.
mahabharata:12:49.77	I must surely repay them; I do not wish for protection by one who is not valiant.
Then Kashyapa, bringing those named by the earth, consecrated those kshatriya kings esteemed for valour.
Their sons and grandsons, whose lines are established—thus is this old story that you ask of me, Pandava."
[Vaishampayana said:] Speaking thus, the hero of the Yadus went swiftly with Yudhishthira, best of the upholders of dharma, in that chariot, like the sun entering the three worlds with its rays.

Ah, the prowess of Rama, Vrishni, great-souled like Shakra, by whom the earth was made free of kshatriyas in anger!
mahabharata:12:50.3	Protected by cows, by the ocean, by langurs, bears and monkeys, the upholders of the families of kshatriyas, afraid of Rama.
mahabharata:12:50.4	Ah, blessed is this world and fortunate the men on earth in which such a righteous deed was done by a Brahmana, Achyuta.
Going so, dear one, those two, Achyuta and Yudhishthira, went to where Gangeya lay on his bed of arrows, the lord.
Then they saw Bhishma lying on his bed of arrows, wrapped in a net of his own rays, like the evening sun, like fire.
Attended by sages as Shatakratu by gods, in a supremely righteous place along the river Oghavati.
Seeing him from afar, Krishna and the king of dharma, the four Pandavas and Sharadvata (Kripa) and the others,
descending from their vehicles, restraining the wavering mind and uniting the host of senses, approached the great sages.
Then, asking the son of Ganga of the growth of his austerity, the Yadus and Kurus, bulls among men, sat down surrounding him.
Then seeing the son of Ganga like a fire being quenched, Keshava, somewhat dejected in mind, said to Bhishma:

Are your knowledges clear as before, O king? Is your intellect untroubled, best of speakers?
mahabharata:12:50.14	Does your body not pain you from the sorrow of the arrow-blows? For bodily pain is stronger than mental.
mahabharata:12:50.15	By your father's boon you have death at will, lord; but this is not a cause of peace for the righteous Shantanu's son.
mahabharata:12:50.16	Even a very small thorn in the body causes pain here; how much more for you covered with showers of arrows, Bharata.
mahabharata:12:50.17	It is true you need not be told of the origin and dissolution of beings; you can instruct even the gods in what is best, Bharata.
mahabharata:12:50.18	Whatever is past, future or present, bull among men, all that is for you, grown old in knowledge, as if in the palm of your hand.
mahabharata:12:50.19	The cycle of beings and the rise of the fruit of dharma are known to you, greatly wise one, for you are a treasure made of Brahma.
mahabharata:12:50.20	I have seen you established in a prosperous kingdom, whole in limb, healthy, surrounded by thousands of women, a celibate.
mahabharata:12:50.21	Except for Bhishma son of Shantanu, truthful, of great valour, a hero devoted to dharma alone, in the three worlds, king,
mahabharata:12:50.22	we have not heard of anyone, dear one, lying on a bed of arrows who has held off death by force and has natural lordship over it.
mahabharata:12:50.23	In truth, austerity, giving, sacrifice, archery, the Veda and constant care,
mahabharata:12:50.24	kind, pure, self-controlled and devoted to the good of all beings, we have not heard of any great chariot-warrior like you.
mahabharata:12:50.25	You alone, in a single chariot, are able to conquer the gods with Gandharvas, the asuras and Rakshasas; there is no doubt.
mahabharata:12:50.26	You, Bhishma, mighty-armed, are among the Vasus like Vasava; ever called by the Brahmanas the ninth, not the lesser, in virtues.
mahabharata:12:50.27	I know who you are, best of men, famed even among the gods, greatly strong by your own power.
mahabharata:12:50.28	Among men, lord of men, I have neither seen nor heard of any man on earth equal to you in virtues.
mahabharata:12:50.29	You surpass even the gods in all virtues, O king, for by austerity you are able to create the worlds, moving and unmoving.
mahabharata:12:50.30	So remove, Bhishma, the grief of this eldest son of Pandu, tormented by the destruction of his kinsmen.
mahabharata:12:50.31	The dharmas declared for the four classes, Bharata, mixed with the four stages of life, all of them are known to you.
mahabharata:12:50.32	What was said about the four Vedas and the four hotri priests, Bharata, and the eternal dharmas fixed in Sankhya and yoga,
mahabharata:12:50.33	and the one dharma that does not conflict with the four classes when practised, that first one, son of Ganga, is known to you.
mahabharata:12:50.34	The Itihasa and Purana are fully known to you, and the whole of the law-books ever stand in your mind.
mahabharata:12:50.35	Whatever matters causing doubt there are in this world, there is no cutter of them but you, bull among men.
mahabharata:12:50.36	Remove with your wisdom the grief that has arisen in the Pandava's mind, O lord of men; for those like you, of supreme and wide intellect, exist for the peace of bewildered people.

Homage to you, revered Vishnu, source of the world's dissolution; you are the doer, Hrishikesha, and the destroyer, unconquered.
mahabharata:12:51.3	Homage to you, Vishvakarman, soul of the universe, source of the universe; you are the release of beings, standing beyond the five.
mahabharata:12:51.4	Homage to you in the three worlds, homage to you in the three dependent ones; homage to you, lord of yoga, for you are the refuge of all.
mahabharata:12:51.5	By the word you speak resting on me, best of men, I see your divine states in the three paths.
mahabharata:12:51.6	And I see in truth that eternal form of yours; the seven paths of the immeasurably radiant Wind are blocked by you.
mahabharata:12:51.7	Your head pervades the sky, the goddess Earth is your feet, the directions your arms, the sun your eye, and Shakra rests in your valour.
mahabharata:12:51.8	We infer your body, flax-flower-hued, clad in yellow, Achyuta, like a cloud with lightning.
mahabharata:12:51.9	To me who have taken refuge in you, a devotee, wishing the desired goal, whatever is best, lotus-eyed one, meditate on that, best of gods.
mahabharata:12:51.12	You are my devotee, ever steadfast in uprightness, devoted to restraint, austerity, truth and giving, pure.
You are worthy, Bhishma, to see me by your own austerity, O king; for the worlds from which one does not return are present for you.
Fifty-six days of your life remain, hero of the Kurus; then, by the rise of the fruit of good deeds, you will unite with them, Bhishma, leaving the body.
These gods, the Vasus, all blazing like fire, mounted on celestial cars, hidden, await you, as the water-bird waits for the sun at its turning.
As soon as the revered Sun has turned to the northern quarter by time's course, you will go, hero among men, to the worlds from which a wise man does not return.
When you, Bhishma, have gone to that other world, all knowledge will perish entirely, hero; therefore we have all come near you to discern dharma.
Tell Yudhishthira, whose knowledge is afflicted by grief for kin, and who is bound to truth, words joined to dharma and wealth and concentration, meaningful, to remove his grief."

Lord of the world, mighty-armed, auspicious Narayana, Achyuta, hearing your words I am flooded with joy.
mahabharata:12:52.3	And what shall I say in your presence, lord of speech, when all speech is contained in your speech?
mahabharata:12:52.4	Whatever is done in the world or is to be done has come forth from you, for the divine worlds are made of your intellect.
mahabharata:12:52.5	He who would speak of the world of the gods near the king of the gods would state to you the meanings of the sciences of dharma, desire and wealth.
mahabharata:12:52.6	My mind is pained by the arrow-blows, Madhusudana, my limbs sink, and my intellect is not clear.
mahabharata:12:52.7	I have no ready thought at all to speak, Govinda, being pierced by arrows like poison and fire.
mahabharata:12:52.8	My strength, my intelligence fail, my life hastens away, my vitals burn, and my mind wanders.
mahabharata:12:52.9	From weakness my speech falters; how can I speak? Be gracious to me, Dasharha, delight of the family.
[Vasudeva said:] "This speech is fitting from the bearer of the Kuru burden, of great valour and great strength, who sees all aims.
As for what you say to me of the pain from arrow-wounds, Gangeya, accept here a boon from me, made by my grace, lord.
You will have no despondency, no faintness, no burning, no pain, Gangeya, nor hunger or thirst."
Fie on Death, the wicked, cruel, causing grief to the good; and I shall slay you too, the sin, the cause of sin.

Seeing the great soul depart, bowing with joined palms, Hari, knowing the destruction of the Vrishnis, did not wish to prevent it.
I do not remember any untruth of his, even in jest, the great soul; what then is the change by which he has fallen to the ground?
Stay, mighty-armed Bharata, even for a moment; while you stay, Kaurava, the torment does not trouble us.
